spots.s: The 1923 horseshoe where the Beatles and Dylan played and the US Open was won — a 14,000-seat concert bowl you can walk home from.
Brick paving, a clock tower and a Tudor archway three minutes from the E/F — the neighborhood's living room, and a summer beer garden under the arch.
Twelve blocks of shops, cafés and restaurants from 69th Road to Ascan — the closest thing Queens has to a main street you'd stroll for its own sake.
A five-screen independent on Metropolitan Avenue with recliners and real beer — first-run films without the Times Square markup.
Where the US Open lived until 1978 — grass courts still played on, and the clubhouse porch visible from Tennis Place.
The triangle where Queens Boulevard meets Yellowstone — chess tables, a greenmarket on Sundays and the neighborhood's default meeting point.
The borough's great park is a 15-minute ride up 108th Street — Unisphere, Meadow Lake, the museums and enough space to lose an afternoon.
A 1903 Daniel Muller carousel, hand-carved and landmarked, running weekends in season at the Woodhaven end of Forest Park.
The multi-level mall a stop up Queens Boulevard — Costco, Century 21 and the parking garage that makes a car-based errand run painless.
39 acres in Flushing with a rose garden, a bee garden and a wedding lawn — twenty minutes on the Q64 and far calmer than the Bronx one.
The arthouse two stops east — documentaries, foreign films and the Sunday matinee crowd that discusses them on the sidewalk after.

events.n: 颜人中 Ele Yan — MOMENTⁿ World Tour
events.s: Mandopop singer Ele Yan 颜人中 plays two nights at Colden Auditorium on the Queens College campus, close to home.
Illusionist Vitaly Beckman's visual magic show plays Queens Theatre Saturday night (8p) and Sunday afternoon (2p), close to home in Flushing Meadows.

events.n: Salcedo's Latin Soul: Pops y Palmas album release
events.s: Saxophonist Steven Salcedo's Caribbean tribute to Louis Armstrong gets its live release in LeFrak Concert Hall at Queens College, a quick trip down Kissena from Forest Hills.

events.n: Keith Michael's The Nutcracker (New York Theatre Ballet)
events.s: An hour-long, Art Nouveau Nutcracker by New York Theatre Ballet at Colden Auditorium, Queens College — the nearest Nutcracker to Austin St.

events.n: Winter Wonder at Queens Botanical Garden
events.s: Queens Botanical Garden's holiday afternoon — live music, a holiday bar, evergreen displays and a lantern walk to the tree lighting, a quick drive up from Forest Hills.

events.n: Handel's Messiah — Queens College Choral Society
events.s: The Queens College Choral Society's 86th annual winter concert brings Messiah to Colden Auditorium, a neighborhood holiday tradition close to Austin St.

events.n: Hidden Altars of Grief and Remembrance
events.s: A moving Día de Muertos–season altar show at the Queens Museum, beside the Unisphere.

events.n: American Hagwon: A Conversation with Min Jin Lee
events.s: The 'Pachinko' author comes home to Queens College's Colden Auditorium to launch her new novel — reading, conversation and signing; tickets bundle the book via Kew & Willow.
Oscar Hernández's Grammy-winning salsa orchestra marks 25 years with a Puerto Rican Christmas set at Colden — plena, bomba and aguinaldos; expect the aisles to dance.

events.n: Lunar New Year: Year of the Fire Goat 羊年 (Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company)
events.s: All-ages Lunar New Year dance show at Colden Auditorium — dragons, lions, peacocks, acrobats and ribbon dancers in a 65-minute program; $15.
LA jazz/neo-soul vocalist with Earth, Wind & Fire lineage plays LeFrak Concert Hall behind his album 'FLY' — layered vocals, R&B warmth, $25.
Queens College dance program at the Goldstein Theatre — house, tap, Asian-fusion and physical theatre by student companies plus guest artist Andrea Gavriliu; $20, Thu–Sat 7p, Sun 3p.

events.n: Monkey King: The Kung Fu Musical 美猴王
events.s: Queens-made musical retelling of Journey to the West at Queens Theatre's Claire Shulman stage — kung fu choreography and a classical-meets-rock score; Sat 1p & 7p, Sun 1p.

eats.s: Thin, blistered, restrained on the cheese, with cannoli filled to order — the reason nobody here takes the subway for pizza.
A soda fountain barely touched since the 1920s — marble counter, house-made ice cream, real whipped cream, cash only.
Whole grilled fish and a long meze list at Austin and 70th — the neighborhood's default celebration dinner for twenty years.
Craft taps, elevated pub food and live bands most weekends, a block from the LIRR platform — the reliable late one on Austin Street.
A small Austin Street steakhouse doing dry-aged cuts and a serious weekend brunch — book it, the dining room seats maybe forty.
Set into the cobbles beside Station Square with a koi pond and a terrace — the prettiest table in the neighborhood on a summer evening.
The Michelin-starred room that put Forest Hills dining on the map, on Metropolitan — small plates, deep wine list, no fuss.
The chain started in Astoria and still does a proper grass-fed burger — the practical family dinner on Austin Street.
Blue-corn tortillas pressed in the room and a lit-up VW bus behind the counter — the easy weeknight table on Austin.
Austin Street's Indian standby — proper tandoor char, generous thalis and a lunch buffet that fills with LIRR commuters.
Cake cases the length of the shop and a café open till midnight — the after-dinner stop that made Metropolitan Avenue a destination.
Rego Park's 1952 knish counter, a mile up Queens Boulevard — potato, kasha or spinach, baked and the size of your fist.
With Rego Park's Ben's Best long gone, the Bayside branch is the nearest proper kosher deli — pastrami, matzo ball soup, dill pickles on the table.
A small Austin Street noodle counter doing tonkotsu and karaage — the cheap, fast, good option when Nick's has a queue.
Metropolitan Avenue's other pizza institution — a proper dining room, a wood oven, and a bar that fills after Little League.
Elmhurst-adjacent Indonesian on Woodhaven — rendang, nasi campur and sambal that actually bites, twenty minutes away.

shops.s: National chains on the west end, independents east of 71st — bookshop, bakeries, opticians and a hardware store all inside eight blocks.
The neighborhood independent, two stops east in Kew Gardens — book clubs, kids' story hours and a shelf of Queens authors.
The nearest Trader Joe's, in Rego Center with parking above — go on a weekday, the Saturday queue reaches the escalator.
Two levels above Queens Boulevard with a cart escalator — the bulk run, the cheapest gas card in the area, and a rotisserie chicken on the way out.
Metropolitan Avenue's organic grocer with a hot bar and a juice counter — the health-food stop that predates the chains by decades.
The big enclosed mall at Woodhaven and Queens Boulevard — practical rather than charming, and open when Austin Street has shut.
Two long-running Austin Street wine merchants a block apart — the one with the handwritten shelf-talkers will pick a bottle for your dinner.
Hand-dipped chocolates made on Metropolitan Avenue since 1930, now under new local owners who kept the copper kettles.
The local wrench for Forest Park trail bikes and Queens Boulevard commuters — flat fixes while you wait, no attitude.
Color matching and quarts for a weekend project, on the boulevard where you can actually park for ten minutes.
The Bukharian and Russian shopfronts along 63rd Drive and 108th — bakeries, delis, jewellers and a produce market that never closes.
An Austin Street staple for pens, cards, printing and school supplies — the shop you only appreciate when you need a padded envelope now.

essentials.s: Keys cut, screens repaired and someone who will walk you to the right aisle — the old-fashioned hardware store the neighborhood still has.
Queens Boulevard's other hardware counter — paint, plumbing fittings and propane swaps within walking distance of Austin Street.
The 108th Street branch with long hours and a photo counter — the default prescription pickup in Forest Hills.
An independent on 108th Street that still compounds, delivers and answers the phone — worth transferring a prescription for.
Consistently among the cheapest posted prices in the area, on Woodhaven just south of Queens Boulevard — cash pricing, so check the sign.
The everyday fill-up on the boulevard with air, a mini-mart and a lit forecourt at 2am.
Members-only pumps beside the Rego Center warehouse — reliably 40-60 cents under the boulevard stations, with a queue to match.
The licensed Austin Street dispensary, open daily till 9p — flower, edibles and vapes, with staff who'll steer you off the strongest shelf.
OCM-licensed on 108th Street, a short drive from Austin — the regulated option among the unlicensed storefronts along the boulevard.
Several vape and tobacco counters cluster between 70th and 72nd — coils, pods and juice within a two-minute walk of the subway.

essentials.n: NYU Langone Urgent Care Forest Hills
essentials.s: Walk-in care on Queens Boulevard seven days a week — the right call when the ER is overkill and the GP is closed.
The Queens Boulevard branch — passport applications by appointment, and a self-service kiosk that works after the counter shuts.
The Metropolitan Avenue branch — free wifi, a quiet reading room and museum passes you can borrow with a library card.
Big-drum machines and wash-and-fold by the pound near Continental Avenue — the answer when the building's basement machine dies again.
A tunnel wash and vacuum bay off Queens Boulevard — the once-a-season strip of winter parkway salt.
E, F, M and R plus the LIRR at Station Square — express to Midtown in 20 minutes, which is the real reason to live here.
Inspections, brakes and tyres a mile up the boulevard — the neighborhood shop people actually recommend to each other.

walks.s: Tudor houses, private lanes and Olmsted-style curves laid out in 1911 — start at Station Square and wander; there is no wrong turn.
3.3 miles of real forest ten minutes from Austin Street — 150-year-old oaks on the terminal moraine and no skyline in sight.
A flat 3-mile circuit of the city's biggest freshwater lake with the Unisphere on the skyline — the default long walk from here.
Walk Metropolitan south past the bakeries and Aigner's, over the LIRR cut, and straight into the park's bridle paths — twenty-five minutes door to trees.
From the Unisphere fountains past the New York State Pavilion and the museums — flat, paved, and full of cricket matches on a Sunday.
A lake, a historic tree grove planted from a 19th-century nursery, and the velodrome — twenty minutes east and rarely crowded.
The planted center malls of Yellowstone through Forest Hills North — benches, big plane trees and a quiet twenty minutes each way.
Over the Union Turnpike bridge into Kew Gardens' Tudor blocks and the wooded Victorian cemetery beyond — an hour, all of it shaded.
The full 4.3-mile wetland-to-forest circuit twenty minutes east, taking in the Queens Giant — the oldest living thing in the city.
Forty minutes down Woodhaven and over the bridge for 5.5 miles of ocean boardwalk — the neighborhood's summer escape valve.

sights.s: An ivy-covered Tudor arch and clock over brick paving, built 1911 to make arriving by train feel like arriving in an English village.
The 1912 hotel block whose ground-floor arcade still runs through to Continental — vaulted, tiled and almost always empty.
140 feet of stainless-steel Earth left from the 1964 World's Fair, fountains running around it all summer — fifteen minutes up 108th Street.
Philip Johnson's saucer towers and the roofless Tent of Tomorrow, rusting since the Fair closed — open a couple of days a year, photogenic always.
Three drained 1850s basins on the Brooklyn border that reforested themselves into a wooded bowl — a bird sanctuary hidden on top of a ridge.
A tiny colonial burying ground marooned on a traffic island at Trotting Course Lane — eighteenth-century Queens, surrounded by parkway.
North America's first traditional Hindu temple, its carved granite gopuram rising off a Flushing side street, with a dosa canteen downstairs.
Fifty-two hand-carved Daniel Muller horses from 1903, landmarked in place — the finest carousel animals left in the city.
The gated stone entrance where Ascan Avenue meets the Gardens, the boundary between ordinary Queens and the private lanes behind it.

A 1948 Streamline Moderne synagogue on Queens Boulevard by Frank Grad & Sons, its facade carrying a mosaic by A. Raymond Katz — on the State and National Registers and a five-minute detour off the boulevard.
The borough's 1940 civic block in Kew Gardens — 580 feet of red-brick stripped classicism opened by Mayor La Guardia, fronted since 2025 by a renovated plaza on Queens Boulevard.

museums.s: The 1939 World's Fair building holding the Panorama of the City of New York — 895,000 model buildings, every one standing before 1992.
Hands-on physics in a Fair-era pavilion with rocket park outside — the reliable rainy-day plan with kids, fifteen minutes north.
Satchmo's Corona house exactly as he left it, turquoise kitchen and all, with the tape archive in a new center across the street.
Astoria's museum of film and television craft, built onto the old Paramount studio — the Jim Henson gallery alone justifies the trip.
47 acres farmed without a break since 1697 — sheep, planting fields and an autumn corn maze, free on ordinary weekdays.
Queens College's own art museum on the fourth floor of Klapper Hall — antiquities to contemporary prints, and a short hop up Kissena Boulevard.
Founding Father Rufus King's farmhouse in the middle of a Jamaica park — hourly tours Tuesday to Saturday on his fight against slavery.
The East Flushing home of the inventor who perfected the carbon light-bulb filament, renovated and reopened as a museum of Black innovation.
Isamu Noguchi's own studio building and walled garden by the East River — basalt, light sculptures and a stillness the rest of the city never manages.
The contemporary-art outpost in a former Long Island City schoolhouse, now free to all — big installations, and the summer Warm Up parties in the courtyard.

nightlife.s: June to September in the 1923 horseshoe — the rare big-name show you can walk home from, with the sound cut at a neighbourly hour.
Craft taps and bands most weekends a block from the LIRR — the reliable late one when you don't want to get on a train.
An Austin Street institution of forty-odd years — cheap pints, a jukebox, and the crowd that has been coming since college.
Metropolitan Avenue's Irish room with matches on the screens and a back room for live sets — the neighborhood's default Friday.
Ridgewood's outdoor dance yard with a Funktion-One rig and a 24-hour weekend license — twenty minutes away and the best floor in Queens.
Astoria's late lounge with DJs Thursday to Saturday and a retractable roof — the nearest proper dance floor without crossing a river.
Astoria cocktails done properly, with a good late kitchen — the grown-up option when Austin Street feels small.
A 50,000-square-foot former door factory in Maspeth running the big-room dance nights and touring DJs — a short cab from Austin Street and worth staying till close.
Richmond Hill's Saturday R&B party in The RnB Room — slow jams into hip-hop and Afrobeats from radio DJs, just over the line from Kew Gardens.
Big Japanese-Latin restaurant by the 30th Ave stop that turns into a dress-up Saturday party — hip-hop, R&B, Afrobeats and dancehall.

chinese.n: Elmhurst Chinatown 艾姆赫斯特华埠
chinese.s: Broadway between Whitney and 45th: Chinese bakeries, Thai groceries and Cantonese roast-meat windows — ten minutes up Queens Boulevard.

chinese.n: Fay Da Bakery 發達餅家
chinese.s: Pineapple buns, egg tarts and cheap iced milk tea — the Elmhurst counter is the closest proper Chinese bakery to Forest Hills.

chinese.n: Shanghai You Garden 上海豫園
chinese.s: Thin-skinned xiao long bao and scallion pancakes in Elmhurst — the soup-dumpling trip that doesn't require going to Flushing.
College Point's Sichuan bench-mark — chong qing chicken, cumin lamb and a mala level they will actually take seriously if you ask.

chinese.n: New World Mall food court 新世界商城
chinese.s: Thirty-plus stalls under Flushing's Main Street mall — hand-pulled noodles, Xi'an burgers and skewers, all for the price of one Manhattan main.

chinese.n: Hong Kong Supermarket 香港超級市場
chinese.s: The Elmhurst branch on Broadway — live tanks, a roast-meat window and the fresh noodle case that makes cooking at home worth it.
A five-story Korean-Chinese bathhouse in College Point — saunas, outdoor pools and a food court, and a full day out for the price of a dinner.
Flushing's newest Asian mall — hot pot, a cinema, a food hall and boba, all under one roof twenty minutes north.

Austin Street's own Sichuan kitchen, two blocks from the subway — get the mortar-and-pestle smashed eggplant, crispy spicy shredded beef and the slow-simmered fish with chilis and soft tofu, and ignore the takeout side of the menu.
Elmhurst's long-running Taiwanese room on Broadway — order fly's head and fried stinky tofu for the table; tea cups stay full, it suits a big group and a late night. Bring cash.
Tiny Dongan Avenue shop for Taiwanese beef noodle soup — beef neck, a heap of spinach and smooth noodles; stir in the pickled mustard greens from the table.

social.s: Hudson Valley growers on the MacDonald Park triangle, plus a compost drop-off — the neighborhood's weekly reason to talk to strangers.
A hundred vendors under the New York State Pavilion with a $6 price ceiling — the friendliest crowd in the borough, fifteen minutes north.
Riders meet at the Metropolitan Avenue entrance for an easy loop of the park drive and the bridle paths — all paces, no drop.
A weekly no-drop run from Austin Street out through the Gardens and back, finishing at whichever bar has room.
Regulars play through the afternoon on the park's stone tables — bring a clock and you'll get a game within ten minutes.
Weekly pub quiz a block from the subway — teams of four, prize bar tab, and the neighborhood's easiest way into a conversation.
Weekend planting and clean-up sessions open to anyone who signs up — free entry, and you meet half of Flushing doing it.
A 1,900-member Meetup that takes over Cobblestones Pub every Tuesday — Carcassonne to Wingspan to heavy Euros, and newcomers get seated straight into a game; $15 food-or-drink minimum.
The Austin Street gastropub's weekly quiz — bring a team of up to eight or play solo; happy hour runs until 7, so arrive early and settle in.

The club's been running Forest Park since 1980: weekend run/walks from Woodhaven Blvd & Park Drive over the trails, roads and track and through the Gardens. All paces; run with them before paying the $10 yearly dues.

remote.s: The neighborhood's own coworking, upstairs at 108-14 72nd Ave — a block off Austin St and the 71st Ave E/F/M/R, two from the LIRR. Two floors of hot desks and couches, a lounge, Wi-Fi, privacy booths, a printer and a conference room. 24/7 on a member card; $45/mo Basic includes one day, extra days $25. Tours by appointment.
remote.b: Chill and not crowded, phone booth usually free, per a member

remote.s: Walkable from Austin St: Regus on the 4th floor of Forest Hills Tower, 118-35 Queens Blvd at the Kew Gardens–Union Tpke express stop. Wi-Fi, printer/scanner, a terrace, kitchen with hot drinks, car and bike parking; book desks or rooms in the Regus app. Staffed M–F 8:30a–5p, members 24/7. The pick when you need a door that closes.
remote.b: Meeting rooms usually available, per a member

remote.s: Cozy café at 68-04 Burns St, by Station Square and the Forest Hills LIRR: fast Wi-Fi, laptops welcome and adequate seating, with a 4.7-star following among locals.
remote.b: Busy, with lines at peak; laptops fill the tables on weekends

remote.s: Café at 72-01 Austin St, a short walk from the 71st Ave E/F/M/R: Wi-Fi, laptops allowed, and spacious, comfortable seating.
remote.b: Laptop-friendly, but a 2-hour limit applies when it's busy

remote.s: The neighborhood branch at 108-19 71st Ave, half a block from the 71st Ave E/F/M/R and the Austin St shops. Free QPL_Wi-Fi, public computers with a library card, quiet reading tables, and museum passes to borrow. Last published hours: Mon, Wed, Thu 10a–8p; Tue 1–6p; Fri 10a–6p; Sat 10a–5:30p — check before a long session.
remote.b: One of the busiest Queens branches; often crowded

remote.s: Yemeni coffeehouse at 107-29 71st Ave (Continental Ave), a few minutes' walk from Austin St: Wi-Fi, tables with outlets, tons of seating and soft Arabic music. Adeni chai, Yemeni coffee and pastries. Opens 6a weekdays (8a weekends) and stays open until 11:30p nightly. Drink waits can top 20 minutes at peak.
remote.b: Lively and often crowded, but the line moves fast; seats free in evenings

iceskating.s: The nearest rink to Forest Hills, a short drive up to the Flushing Meadows Aquatic Center, with public skating every day of the year. Weekday daytime sessions run 10:30a–5:15p (from 9a on Fridays), and weekends are noon–4:45p plus Friday and Saturday nights. Admission is $5 on Mondays, $8 other weekdays and $12 weekends, and rentals are $7.

A rooftop NHL rink in Long Island City, a quick run up the LIE. Hockey and classes fill most of the ice, and the regular public skate (Sundays 1:10–2:50p, $12) isn't offered from July to December, so in late fall look for holiday-week sessions instead. Rentals are $8, bring your own helmet, and parking in its garage is free.

Prospect Park's pair of rinks, one covered and one open-air, is a pretty half-day trip. The open-air rink opens Nov 15 and runs 9a–6p daily. Mondays cost $5, other weekdays $10, and nights, weekends and holidays $15; rentals are $10. Public sessions are for easy laps only, with no spins, jumps or backward skating.

The postcard skate in Central Park, open every day from Oct 28, 2026 to Mar 16, 2027, starting at 10a. Off-Peak days are the cheapest on its tiered calendar, and the WRAP program discounts walk-up entry for IDNYC or NYC library card holders. Community Days are free, including Mar 14–16 at season's end.

Free to skate in the middle of Midtown: a 17,000 sq ft rink open 8a–10p from Oct 28, 2026 to Feb 28, 2027, with the Winter Village shops around it. Rentals range from about $19 to $64 by demand, so bringing your own skates saves the most. Reserve online, and leave bags at home, since they aren't allowed on the ice.

A Williamsburg waterfront rink facing the Manhattan skyline, open Nov 9, 2026 to Feb 21, 2027. Weekday sessions run 2:30–9p and weekend sessions 10:30a–10p, with full days over Dec 23–Jan 3. Book a time slot and arrive 10 minutes early. Stretch Pizza is on the square for after.

The Islanders' two-rink practice facility in Eisenhower Park, about a half-hour east on Long Island, sells public skate tickets at $16, with $7 rentals. Sessions are added each month and often sell out, and very few tickets are sold at the rink, so buy online before you drive.

Central Park's north-end rink at the Harlem Meer runs Community Skate from November. It's the budget pick: adults pay $5 on weekdays before 5p and $10 at peak times, kids pay $5, rentals are $10 and sessions last 80 minutes. Saturday-night Harlem Nights adds a live DJ.

skating.s: The neighborhood's own skate park, inside Forest Park at the Greenhouse Playground: grind rails, quarter pipes, launch ramps, wall rides, a fly box and a half-pipe. Roller blades, roller skates and skateboards only (no bikes). It's open dawn to dusk with no attendant, and you need a helmet and knee and elbow pads.

The closest long, flat skate to Austin St: two paved paths around Meadow Lake in Flushing Meadows, 2.5–3 mi a lap. The pavement is mostly good, but watch for sand and mud along the west shore, and expect wind off the open water. Speed skaters should avoid it in poor light.

North of the LIE from Meadow Lake, the paths around the Unisphere are excellent and the brick walk circling it is in good shape, with a few short step sets nearby for practice. It's lit at night. On summer weekends, fountain spray and the crowds on the east lawns are the only drawbacks.

A bigger step up from Forest Park's ramps: Flushing Meadows' 16,000 sq ft street park, built for the 2010 Maloof Money Cup over the Astral Fountain, with stairs, rails, ledges, pyramids and banks of every size. Inline skates are welcome (no BMX), it's free and unsupervised, dawn to dusk, and pads and a helmet are required.

For an ocean-air skate, head down Woodhaven and Cross Bay to the Rockaway boardwalk, now concrete after its rebuild. Parks' beach rules ban rollerblading only 10a–6p on summer weekends (May 1–Sep 30), so from October to April you can skate any time the boardwalk is open.

Prospect Park's Lakeside rinks run roller skating in summer. The season closed Oct 18, 2026, and the 2027 schedule comes out in March. Last summer's sessions ran daily, with Friday and Saturday nights to 10p; admission was $10 on weekdays, $15 on weekends and $5 on Mondays, with $10 rentals.

The year-round indoor option, over the line in Bushwick: a 7,000 sq ft hand-painted maple floor with a serious sound system, plus music, shows and a bar. Rental skates and pads go first come, first served, and inline skaters are welcome on their own wheels. Sessions vary, so check the calendar.

For skating with a crowd, the city's biggest weekly group skate leaves Union Square's south steps at 8p every Wednesday from April to October: 12–15 mi of city streets at a moderate pace, back by about 10:15p. A smaller, faster winter edition keeps going from November to March.
